Relatives of those being held hostage spent anxious hours as the situation unfolded
Colombian security forces have freed around 76 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.
Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 local time (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella described as a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money.
They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.
With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, de la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, killing one gunman.
Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.
Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage-takers. Four have been arrested.
Around 20 people were still being held hostage when the security forces moved in
De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".
He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation personally. He could be seen flanked by the commanders of the operation with a handgun strapped to his belt, in footage released following its conclusion.
De la Espriella said the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in but had refused.
Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of the hostages, among them elderly women.
But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, located in a popular shopping centre.
Local media report that, as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.
De la Espriella said they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob a cash-laden armoured car had been foiled.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Johan Correa, one of the rescued hostages, described to local media how the gunmen, who he said had been disguised, had entered the supermarket, where he worked.
"We had just started our shift when some guys dressed as police officers came in and started robbing the place," he said. "They were robbers, but we thought they were police."
He added that he and other hostages had been locked in a cold storage room, face down with their hands tied.
"We were there for more than four hours, lying on the floor with our hands tied, and it was a really tough experience."
Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, told Caracol radio that the assailants wore masks and had been armed with guns and knives.
Velázquez said the gunmen repeatedly threatened the hostages, telling them that they had rigged the exits with explosives.
Relatives and bystanders congregated outside the entrance to the supermarket
He said that "thank God" they had been rescued, describing moments of tension as they heard explosions and a helicopter flying above.
Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people kneel with their hands behind their heads.
It is unclear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers.
Local media report that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded.
The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.
The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.
Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces.
A woman called Sandra told Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage.
Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.
Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.
But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.
At one point, flights into the city were halted, with planes diverted to Barranquilla.
Special forces, including units specialised in dealing with kidnappings, were deployed to Cartagena, a popular destination among foreign and Colombian tourists.
Cartagena's Mayor Dumek Turbay called for calm but the granddaughter of one of the hostages told Colombian newspaper El Tiempo that "this shows we're not safe anywhere".
De la Espriella was elected earlier this year on a promise to crack down on Colombia's criminal groups.
He had travelled to the central city of Villavicencio to inspect the damage caused by a car bomb that detonated outside the regional government's offices on Tuesday.
While de la Espriella blamed the leader of a dissident rebel group for that attack, he was adamant that the hostage takers were "simple bandits" without political affiliations.

The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.
Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.
Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.
The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.
Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.
Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.
If you want to get Kagi Mail without the $25 per month subscription, you can subscribe for $9 per month or $99 per year, and there’s a 60-day trial right now.
That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.
According to the company, Kagi Search has just over 75,000 paying subscribers. Compared to the number of people using Google Search or even Bing or DuckDuckGo, that’s not much. But the pitch is that with Google, the user is the product, not the customer, and that paying anywhere from $5 to $25 per month (there are multiple plans; unlimited search queries is in the $10 per month plan) helps users escape from that devil’s bargain.
Kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives. On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago. A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very big part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.
The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail. That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative and sensible. (You can disable either Gemini in Gmail or Kagi’s AI features in Kagi Mail, too.)
Email is also different because there are already more direct competitors to Kagi Mail. The most popular in this category is Proton Mail, which goes even further on privacy and security with end-to-end encryption, but that company is embroiled in controversies right now. There’s also Tuta, which Kagi specifically flags and praises in its blog post as a good existing alternative.
Based on a few hours of use, Kagi Mail seems like it’s going in the right direction, but it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail. Your needs may vary, but there are many good reasons to consider alternatives to Google’s business model and products.

Musician who had huge 1980s chart success had been diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2018
Andy Taylor, the guitarist with 80s pop megastars Duran Duran , has died aged 65.
He had been diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, which he disclosed publicly in 2022 when Duran Duran were about to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” read a statement shared with Variety . “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.”
A statement from Duran Duran added: “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”
Taylor was born in 1961 and grew up in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in a family who worked in the local fishing industry. He began playing guitar from the age of 11 and was tutored by Dave Black of the David Bowie backing band the Spiders from Mars. He left school early to start playing in bands on the working men’s club scene.
In 1980 he joined the nascent Duran Duran, who had formed in 1978 but whose lineup was far from settled – they advertised for a guitarist in Melody Maker, and Taylor travelled to Birmingham to audition. “A couple of days later they rang me and said out of 40 or so I was the only one who knew how to tune up, let alone play,” he later recalled.
The following month Simon Le Bon joined as frontman, by February 1981 they had released their debut single Planet Earth, and with the July release of Girls on Film – a song propelled by Taylor’s ultra-tight and rhythmic playing – they became major stars in the UK and US. Rio, their second album released in 1982, cemented their international playboy image and went Top 10 in both countries, and follow-up Seven and the Ragged Tiger topped the UK chart. Speaking to Smash Hits in 1983, Taylor described his new-found career as “a hobby gone mad”. That year Taylor also opened a wine bar called Rio, in Whitley Bay in his native Tyneside.
Following their third album Duran Duran went on a brief hiatus, during which time Taylor and bassist John Taylor (no relation) formed a new funk-rock group, the Power Station, with singer Robert Palmer and former Chic drummer Tony Thompson. Two singles, the original track Some Like It Hot and a cover of T Rex’s Get It On, reached the US Top 10 in 1985.
Later that year Taylor rejoined Duran Duran to record A View to a Kill, the US chart-topping James Bond film theme, and perform with them at Live Aid in Philadelphia. But amid drug use, relations had become strained: drummer Roger Taylor left due to exhaustion, and Andy Taylor himself left to pursue the rockier direction he began with the Power Station – though his Duran Duran bandmates initially believed he would be continuing with the band.
“I’d come close to a nervous breakdown from the stresses of our crazy life and my own cocaine problem,” Taylor later said. “Combine that with all the shouting matches and the icy silences – I just knew I had to get out. So I did. The day after Live Aid, I stopped drinking and taking drugs. And I quietly started getting legal advice on extricating myself from Duran Duran.”
Collaborating with Sex Pistols’ Steve Jones, he released a solo LP, Thunder, in 1986, and the single Take It Easy was a minor US hit. As well as recording a covers album, Dangerous, he spent a number of years as a writer and producer for hire, with his song Lost in You becoming a transatlantic hit for Rod Stewart in 1988.
The Power Station briefly reunited in 1996, and then in 2000, the classic lineup of Duran Duran reformed and released a new album together, Astronaut, in 2004. He also toured with the band and worked on another (later scrapped) album Reportage, but was hit hard by the death of his father to cancer, and left the band again in 2006; he was diagnosed with depression the following year.
He spent the next decade away from music, first publishing his memoir Wild Boy: My Life in Duran Duran in 2008. He released a new solo single in 2019 and joined British rock band Reef as a tour guitarist, also producing their 2022 album Shoot Me Your Ace.
Despite the at-times fractious relationship with Duran Duran over the years, Taylor said in his statement accompanying the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction that there was no “bad blood … just pure love and respect for everything we wrote, recorded and achieved together”.
He married his wife Tracey Wilson in 1982, and they had four children together: Andrew, Georgina, Bethany and Isabella.
Following his cancer diagnosis, he credited his successful music career with keeping him upbeat. “I’ve been very fortunate, I’ve had so much, in terms of living the dream, but because I do music, I think that’s probably really helped me to live with pessimism of an incurable disease,” he said.

Unclear if ‘hostage-taker’ who was killed may have been a hostage as daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre ends
Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one man police described as a hostage-taker was killed.
Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.
When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8am on Tuesday local time, customers and employees were taken hostage – the president initially said there were 30 hostages, but after the final count, police put the number at about 70.
Many of them could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.
When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested.
One man was killed, whom De la Espriella and police described as one of the criminals who had allegedly resisted.
“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” said De la Espriella in a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year.
Local media identified the dead man as Haider Muñetón Zapata, 51, whose wife had spent the day searching for him as one of the hostages. She gave an interview to Blu Radio on Tuesday, saying they lived near the supermarket and that he had gone there to buy buñuelos, a type of fried dough ball, before picking her up to take her to work, but had stopped responding to her WhatsApp messages at 8.12am.
Zapata reportedly had no criminal record. Cartagena’s mayor, Dumek Turbay, told local media that when special forces stormed the supermarket, Zapata had allegedly resisted and attacked one of the officers, prompting police to shoot him dead.
In a video released shortly after the operation, De la Espriella described the police action as “extraordinary”, speaking with a gun tucked into his waistband, as he has done on several other public occasions as part of his populist tough-on-crime rhetoric.
The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.
The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.
As the lengthy negotiations continued into the night, police used water cannon to disperse dozens of onlookers who had gathered outside the supermarket.
Cartagena’s mayor said that when police stormed the supermarket, some of the hostage-takers tried to blend in with the hostages by removing their hoods and changing out of their black clothes into civilian clothing.
According to Turbay, police then had to screen the hostages before eventually identifying the four who were arrested.
Supermarket employee Héctor Puello, who was taken hostage, told Caracol Radio that he had started his shift in the store’s bakery about two and a half hours before the gunmen arrived.
“First of all, I felt like I had come back to life because those armed men were mistreating us,” he said.
Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, said that when he realised what was happening, he hid inside a cold-storage room with four other employees. “After four hours, we couldn’t stand the cold any longer and came out,” he said, at which point they were captured and taken hostage.
Commenting on the rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.
The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.
In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.
Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.
On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.
“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

The judges’ recommendations came as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival.
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for an immediate end to his long-running corruption trial after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping a case in which he is accused of bribery.
Netanyahu on Wednesday said the “fabricated cases” against him were falling apart, in a televised statement at the Israeli parliament.
The judges’ recommendations came as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival after inconclusive October 27 elections.
Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot , has been tasked with forming a government, and if Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, he would lose his leverage to avoid a potential jail sentence.
“Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family,” Netanyahu said in his speech.
“Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul. Who will give those years back to us?”
During a hearing in Jerusalem on Wednesday regarding three corruption cases against Netanyahu, judges recommended dropping one, reconsidering another and suggested resolving the third through an agreement, Israeli media reported.
In Case 4000, in which Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, judges indicated there was little chance of a conviction.
That case is considered to be the most serious Netanyahu faces and involves him allegedly offering regulatory favours for a telecoms company in exchange for favourable media coverage.
Netanyahu is alleged to have negotiated with Shaul Elovitch, the controlling shareholder of Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq, to get positive coverage on his Walla news site in exchange for policies benefitting Bezeq.
On Wednesday, Israeli media reported Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman saying that proving the bribery charge in that case faced “considerable difficulties”.
Netanyahu, who has been in power on and off for three decades, has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and denounced the cases as a politically motivated plot against him.
He is the first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial.
Israel’s Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who was unusually summoned to the hearing on Wednesday, said she would consider the judges’ recommendations and was ready for either a verdict or a plea deal.
In Case 2000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over an alleged deal with the owner of Yediot Aharonot for favourable coverage in exchange for curbs on rival newspaper Israel Hayom. Judges on Wednesday questioned whether his actions constituted a crime and recommended reconsidering the case.
In Case 1000, Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust over allegedly accepting luxury gifts from wealthy individuals in exchange for favours. Judges recommended reaching an agreement to conclude the case.
Netanyahu’s right-wing allies cheered the court’s recommendations and demanded the trial be brought to an end.
“After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was flawed from the outset,” Israel Katz, who is the defence minister in Netanyahu’s caretaker government, wrote on X.
During his most recent term, which started in late 2022, Netanyahu proposed far-reaching judicial reforms that critics say sought to weaken the courts.
With coalition negotiations under way, Eisenkot’s camp is already trying to start unravelling some of the Netanyahu-era judicial reforms in parliament.
The presidential contender is expected to meet Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday evening.
His centrist Yashar party said a day earlier that it had agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
Lieberman has ruled out forming a coalition with Arab-led parties that could hand them a majority in parliament. That has frustrated Democrats chief Yair Golan, who has been pushing Eisenkot to reach a deal with parties representing Israel’s 21 percent Arab minority to make good on his campaign promise to bring down Netanyahu.
Eisenkot also faced a new challenge on Tuesday after the left-wing Democrats suspended coalition talks, further complicating his potential path to power.
The Yashar party leader has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.

Kilmar Abrego García, a Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation from the United States put him at the centre of a controversy over US President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, arrived in Madrid on Wednesday.
His case became a focal point in the debate over Trump's mass deportation policy in 2025, raising concerns about migrants' rights to challenge deportation orders and the administration's compliance with court rulings.
Wearing sunglasses and a baseball cap, Abrego García made his way to a vehicle at Madrid airport without speaking to reporters gathered at the scene, according to AFP journalists.
"While details remain private, Kilmar is planning on hosting various international speaking engagements, with stops planned in different countries," We Are CASA, a US immigrant advocacy group which has been supporting him, said in a statement.
The Salvadoran ultimately left the United States voluntarily on a commercial flight bound for Spain.
"I am leaving happy, I am leaving with my freedom," he said in a statement released by We Are CASA.
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed his departure from the country in a statement, in which it labelled Abrego García a "trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator."
"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, quoted in the statement.
His lawyers, for their part, welcomed the fact that their client had been able to leave "on his own terms" after his long-running dispute with the US immigration authorities.
One of his legal representatives, Simón Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the departure brought an end to a deportation campaign he described as "retaliation". He also stressed that the move to Spain is temporary and that Abrego García, who is married to a US citizen, hopes to return to the United States once Donald Trump leaves the White House.
His case began in March 2025, when federal agents arrested Abrego García in the street. Days later he was deported to El Salvador and sent to the Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), a controversial maximum-security mega-prison built on the orders of President Nayib Bukele and intended to house alleged members of criminal gangs.
The deportation went ahead even though there was a court order expressly prohibiting his deportation to El Salvador, where he had received threats from armed groups before leaving the country. The US government itself later acknowledged that it had been "a mistake", although it initially resisted facilitating his return.
Back in the United States, Abrego García reported having suffered beatings, sleep deprivation and psychological torture during the almost three months he was held in CECOT.
The legal battle reached the US Supreme Court, which ordered the Trump administration to facilitate his return. The authorities eventually brought him back to the country, although they did so in the context of a criminal investigation that led to an indictment over his alleged involvement in a migrant-smuggling network.
However, a federal judge ultimately dismissed all the charges, ruling that the indictment was in fact motivated by a desire to retaliate against the Salvadoran for having opposed his deportation.
As the criminal case progressed, the US government continued trying to deport him from the country. The authorities considered sending him to Uganda, Ghana and Eswatini, but failed to secure agreement from those countries to receive him. Meanwhile, Abrego García applied for asylum to prevent his deportation.
The dispute became one of the most high-profile cases under Trump's immigration policy and highlighted the differences between the executive and judicial branches over the limits of presidential powers regarding deportations.
Throughout the process, the US president and several members of his administration publicly accused the Salvadoran of belonging to Mara Salvatrucha, also known as MS-13, as well as of human trafficking and assaulting his wife, all allegations that were echoed in the statement published on Tuesday by the DHS announcing his departure from the country.
However, these accusations were called into question by the courts. In fact, federal judge Paula Xinis, who oversaw part of the litigation in Maryland, went so far as to open a contempt-of-court inquiry against some of the prosecutors involved in the case for allegedly repeatedly disobeying her orders.
Now, with Madrid as his first stop, Abrego García plans to travel to other countries to take part in various events and speak about his experience, according to Sandoval-Moshenberg.

Leah Blyth, federal Liberal senator for South Australia, has announced she is defecting to One Nation , becoming the party’s first upper-house member for the state.
Blyth, a member of Angus Taylor’s frontbench, said she did not believe the Coalition was capable of opposing the Albanese government, which was “running the country into the ground”.
“I can no longer in good conscience tell Australians that the Liberal Party can save this country,” she said in a statement.
“Australia is a country worth fighting for … I want our children to grow up proud of their country, with the freedom and opportunity to build a better life.
“One Nation has never shied away from confronting the uncomfortable truths facing our nation. They are the only party with the bold ideas needed to turn this country around.”
Blyth replaced former Liberal cabinet minister Simon Birmingham in the Senate in 2025. The conservative senator served as a shadow assistant minister for defence infrastructure under Taylor.
She was also the immediate past state president of the Liberal party in South Australia, and was replaced by conservative powerbroker Alex Antic.
Guardian Australia understands the pair, who were previously allies in the conservative faction, had experienced a falling out. Blyth will face re-election at the next poll and was expected to lose her winnable spot on the Senate ticket.
Pauline Hanson welcomed the South Australian senator and said she would “build on One Nation’s expanding support within the state”.
Hanson posted a video to social media on Wednesday night, cooking a steak in a sandwich press and asked viewers to “guess who this is for”.
It was a reference back to the same meal shared between the One Nation leader and then-Nationals MP Barnaby Joyce before his defection.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
On Thursday morning, the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, called Blyth’s defection “disappointing on a number of levels” and condemned the move as part of a broader pattern of behaviour from One Nation.
The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, similarly described the move as a “disappointing decision” but said Blyth “wasn’t a big contributor to the party room”.
Speaking to Radio National, Canavan said the move took him by surprise.
“I try and be friends with everyone … and I thought I was friends with Leah, but there was no warning from her.”
Speaking to Blyth’s reasoning that her values aligned closer to One Nation, Cavanan said the move “smacks of self-interest to me”.
“Good luck to her. Leah went to the election last year supporting net zero. She didn’t oppose the hate speech laws earlier this year, like we did – the Nationals.
“To turn around now a few months later and say, ‘My principles and policies are more aligned with One Nation’ – I mean, give me a break.”

Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.
The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.
It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.
The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.
It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months , external .
It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.
Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.
The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill.
Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.
Customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy they use and how they pay for it.
For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p
Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine
Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas
The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs will not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.
Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.
As well as how much energy you use and how you pay for it, where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.
The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.
The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.
In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.
Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.
Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.
Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.
Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region , external and payment method.
Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers are 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.
From January, daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.
The electricity standing charge is lower than the amount charged over the previous three months, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.
Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.
The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen
Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.
You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind.
Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees.
Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills.
Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households.
However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising.
In December 2025, Ofgem approved a £28bn investment to improve the electricity and gas grids in Great Britain to strengthen energy supplies and protect customers against volatile energy prices. It will also reduce Britain's dependence on gas.
Customers will pay part of the cost of the upgrade, through an additional £108 added to energy bills by 2031.
These charges started to appear from April 2026, adding about £6 a month to the bill for a typical household covered by the energy cap.
High electricity bills targeted in planned shakeup to energy pricing
Households could get free electricity for doing washing on sunny weekends
Suppliers must offer customers affordable payment plans or repayment holidays if they are struggling to pay their bills. Most also offer hardship grants.
Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, and since then unpaid bills and charges have shot up.
Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, has advice for people who may be struggling:
Look closely at how much energy you are using, and be alert to estimated bills, which might prove to be inaccurate.
It is often best to try to talk to someone who can fully understand your situation.
Heating oil is not covered by the energy cap. About 1.5 million UK households use heating oil and they have already seen a sharp increase in bills since the Middle East conflict triggered a jump in oil prices. Some users have seen costs more than double.
The issue is particularly acute in Northern Ireland, where about 500,000 homes use heating all, almost two-thirds of all households.
In March, the government announced a £53m support package to help low-income households in rural communities who use heating oil.

Army hails Iowa’s lead azide detonation, claiming no traces of airborne lead have been detected so far.
United States Army officials have hailed Wednesday’s mission to destroy 68 drums of volatile lead azide — a sensitive munitions explosive — at a military base in Iowa as a success, saying it had “wildly exceeded their expectations”.
Speaking at a news conference in Middletown, a southeastern rural city adjacent to the ammunition plant where the operation was carried out, Major General Eric Shirley, the Army official in charge of the disposal effort, said overhead footage showed that “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed”.
The controlled detonation at 10:15am (16:15 GMT) destroyed approximately 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I.
“There was no secondary explosions. There was no kick-out. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley said, adding that the operation was “tremendously successful”.
Officials also said that extensive mitigation measures, including earthworks, foam barriers and gel blocks, had helped to absorb the shockwaves and toxic fallout.
However, Democratic Illinois House Representative Mike Quigley voiced dissatisfaction over how military leaders handled the operation, calling the holiday-eve scheduling and lack of communication “unconscionable”.
In a statement on X, the congressman wrote: “It is unfair that our military leaders are releasing 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide on our friends in Iowa the day before Thanksgiving.”
Following days of heightened alarm over lead dust contamination and its environmental repercussions, federal officials announced that preliminary data from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sensors had detected no airborne lead particles.
Ongoing monitoring efforts continue in the immediately affected blast zone.
A post on the agency’s social media account shortly after the operation said that “ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region”.
Chemists have noted that lead, as a nonbiodegradable element, cannot be chemically decomposed or destroyed. It persists in the environment, with airborne particles capable of travelling considerable distances before settling on soil and potentially leaching into groundwater.
Detonating large stores of the unstable explosive would decompose the compound into its basic elements – nitrogen gas and metallic lead.
Lead is a potent neurotoxin that poses its sharpest threat to children and pregnant women, with links to learning disabilities, impaired neurological function, mental health challenges, reproductive harm, hearing loss and other impairments.
“The EPA can do millions of tests, but they [must also] test for the breakdown products and the stabilisers and plasticisers [containing] lead azide [which] are endocrine disruptors; some are cancer-causing chemicals,” said Scott Smith, an independent environmental testing expert who was heavily involved in air testing after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment and industrial incidents.
The Army Sustainment Command said it would release a final breakdown of the affected area — including lead-dust dispersion and surface-deposition maps — after the operation.
“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanely possible the risk to the health and the safety of the people in Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Shirley.

Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating bills
Energy bills will soar by 26% in the new year as the war in Iran pushes up wholesale prices.
Typical household bills will rise by £37 per month as Ofgem's latest price cap comes into force from January to March, but experts say it is possible to keep rising bills in check.
Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.
So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.
With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.
turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently
turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use
turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum
These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.
Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.
Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem.
Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.
Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.
Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.
Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.
The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.
Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.
So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.
Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available , not just what your own supplier is offering.
The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.
There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes .
This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill.
Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.
Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment , external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.
Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme , external can help you repay energy debt.
You can get more advice from Ofgem , external , Citizens Advice , external , or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes , external .
People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.
But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.
How is the cost of energy affecting your quality of life? What questions do you have?
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820:
Domestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.
With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?
The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.
Kelly Anne Harvey uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms to save on the central heating
Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.
The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000.
She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.
The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.
To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill .
The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.
They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.
"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.
Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing
Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.
The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year.
Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.
She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.
She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.
"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."
Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.
"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.
"At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."
To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.
Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.
Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.
Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm20:
Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.
A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter.
A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem.
The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.
Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.
Ofgem said the rise had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war. Wholesale gas prices , paid by suppliers, were up 33% in the last three months, the period used to set the January to March cap. They have more than doubled since late 2025.
The warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.
"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.
Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said it wrote to energy suppliers "reminding them of their responsibilities" to customers this winter. They have been told to identify people who need help early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable.
Campaign Groups Friends of the Earth and Global Witness said major oil and energy companies are making huge profits because of spiralling oil costs, hurting households.
Energy UK, which represents suppliers, said the firms which send your bill, have profits capped on a percentage basis and do not see the same benefit as international energy generating companies. However, higher bills will mean higher profits in nominal cash terms.
The increase is the biggest since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest.
People on prepayment meters will be hit as their spending comes when energy is needed, rather than the cost being spread over the year as with direct debits.
The cap sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, not the total bill. Those on fixed deals are unaffected until the end of their term, but for those on variable tariffs it means:
For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p. The electricity price is often pegged to gas, owing to gas-fired generation.
Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine.
Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.
The cap is set every three months, based on the costs faced by suppliers as well as the cost of running the energy system.
It is based on a three-month period that ends about six weeks before the new cap comes into force. A fall in international wholesale prices in recent days will not be reflected in January's cap, but it will be in April's.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills.
"For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets," she said.
Andrew Bowie, shadow energy secretary, said: "It is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes onto bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher.
Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing
Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, said dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.
She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.
She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house.
'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment from 4 January to help with their energy bills this winter, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales.
Citizens Advice said the money will disappear quickly, particularly for those on prepayment meters, leading to a wave of requests for emergency help.
Energy UK said the funding was poorly targeted and insufficient to stem rising levels of customer debt.
The government said councils had a £100m discretionary fund to support vulnerable households which fell outside of the main scheme.

Russia launched scores of drones at energy and civilian targets across Ukraine overnight on Wednesday, killing at least seven people in six regions, authorities said.
The attack involved 112 Shahed, Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, of which 88 were shot down or neutralised, Ukraine's air force said.
One person was killed in Bila Tserkva in Kyiv region, where the strike damaged critical infrastructure, an Epicentr shopping centre and a Nova Poshta postal branch, local authorities said.
One person was killed and seven injured in Kharkiv region after a strike hit a minibus on a highway, regional governor Oleh Synehubov said. Two people aged 76 and 69 were killed and another wounded in Sumy region.
Two people were killed in Odesa region on Tuesday evening — a 41-year-old and a 17-year-old — and one person was killed and three wounded in Zhytomyr region. Casualties were also reported in Chernihiv and Donetsk regions.
Russian forces struck a Naftogaz gas production facility in the Poltava region, the acting head of the company Serhiy Fedorenko said.
A fire broke out and the facility suspended operations. "This is not the first such attack and, unfortunately, not the last," Fedorenko said, adding that Russia was deliberately targeting gas production "to deprive Ukrainians of heat in winter."
Energy facilities in the Dnipropetrovsk region were also hit, triggering emergency power cuts across several districts.
A significant number of consumers lost power in Zaporizhzhia region, Zaporizhzhyaoblenergo head Andriy Stasevskyi said. More than 9,000 customers were left without electricity in Odesa region following Tuesday evening's attacks, regional governor Oleh Kiper said.
The energy company DTEK reported a large-scale strike on one of its thermal power plants, causing serious damage and forcing it to stop generating electricity. DTEK did not specify the location, noting it was the third large-scale strike on its plants in November.
Ukrainian drones simultaneously struck three Russian oil refineries overnight, hitting plants in Samara and Rostov regions, according to Ukrainian monitoring sources.
Two refineries in Samara region — the Kuibyshev and Syzran plants, both part of Rosneft — were struck, with fires breaking out at both facilities.
Regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed the attack but did not name the facilities, saying one person was killed, power had been cut in several districts and a number of schools would operate on an adjusted schedule.
Regional authorities said 145 drones were shot down over the Samara region. Euronews could not independently verify these claims.
The Syzran refinery has a processing capacity of 8.5 million tonnes of oil per year and produces petrol, diesel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil and bitumen.
The Kuibyshev refinery has a primary processing capacity of 8.8 million tonnes per year. Ukraine last struck the Syzran plant on 15 September. The Kuibyshev refinery was also struck that month.
The third refinery struck overnight was the Novoshakhtinsk plant in Rostov region. Regional governor Yuri Slyusar confirmed the attack, saying a combined strike of more than 50 drones and missiles lasted six hours before the plant suspended operations.
Russian oil refining volumes have fallen by an estimated 45% since late October, according to analysts.
Ukraine's General Staff also reported overnight strikes on the Savasleyka airbase in Nizhny Novgorod region, which it described as one of Russia's key aviation facilities and the base from which aircraft carrying Kinzhal missiles launch strikes on Ukrainian cities.
According to Kyiv's military, three MiG-31 and two Su-34 aircraft were damaged and would be unable to fly "for some time".
Ukraine destroyed a span of the road section of the Crimean Bridge last week, halting car traffic, though train services have been restored.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike was a response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, describing deep strikes inside Russia as "long-range sanctions".
Ukraine attacked the bulk carrier Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, claiming it transported military cargo. The following day it struck the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi. Zelenskyy confirmed the warship had been sunk.
On Tuesday, Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened Ukraine with retaliation for its strikes on refineries and complained that Kyiv had not heeded calls from US President Donald Trump to halt attacks on oil processing facilities.
Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was prepared to stop striking Russian refineries only if Moscow halted its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Englishman hailed by teammates and manager Mourinho after coming on to completely change Champions League game against PSV Eindhoven
“I t was one of those moments when you’re just: ‘Wow.’” Bernardo Silva had a good view of Jude Bellingham scoring the goal, the golazo , that put Real Madrid into the lead and the Bernabéu on its feet, shock giving way to song, naa, naa, naa, na-na-na-naa, na-na-na-naa ringing round again. “I have no idea what I did,” the Englishman said afterwards. What he did was turn all Le Tissier. Lifting the ball with his left, raising it with his right, twisting and not letting it drop, he sent it arching from the outside of his boot into the far corner, something straight out of the 90s.
“I just kind of hit it,” Bellingham reckoned; not wanting to hit it too hard, it had gone “looping”, “stabbing”, he said. “Normally [my goals are] a lot closer, aren’t they? I was a bit surprised, honestly. Normally from there I’m looking to see who is an option to play it through to, but it popped up nicely. It was nice.” Nice? It was, Silva said, “special”. A “work of art” Marca called it. The presenter on one radio station claimed it was the best goal he had ever seen, and it wasn’t just him; wasn’t just the goal, either.
“I thought, maybe wrongly, that we could win without Bellingham,” José Mourinho admitted afterwards. The Englishman had what Madrid’s manager called an “almost injury” but at half-time, with Madrid a goal down against PSV Eindhoven and thankful it was just one, he had decided that he had to go on anyway. He had also given them what Bellingham called a “kick up the backside we needed”. Fifteen minutes later, Bellingham was standing there, arms wide. Madrid were 2-1 up; by the end it was 5-1, Bellingham setting Vinícius Júnior free for the fifth.
He had been “absolutely devastating”, Mourinho said. Some injury: everywhere and everything, he had transformed them all, Madrid growing in what El País called “the burning light of Bellingham’s sun”. Marca led on: “Jude resuscitates Real Madrid .” “Bellingham stages a festival,” said AS, Tomás Roncero calling him “the Colossus of Stourbridge”. He had been Polyphemus, El Mundo reckoned. The veteran journalist Alfredo Relaño described him as the closest thing to Alfredo Di Stéfano in “how he runs the game, spreading optimism to everyone”.
Then there was Zinedine Zidane, whose number he has inherited and with whom the comparisons were everywhere. During the game on Tuesday night he had “Zidaned”, Marca said, and so did pretty much everyone else. After the game, the same name was put to him. “It’s a bit much that, eh,” Bellingham replied. “Zidane is much better than me, much more elegant. He is my idol.”
Actually, Bellingham has matched Zidane for leagues and Champions Leagues at Real Madrid already. And, as Jorge Valdano was swift to point out, it’s not just that he might be the best midfielder in the world right now; it’s that he’s still just 23. In theory, there’s a decade more of this; in theory, Bellingham’s prime is still to come.
Set to extend his contract to 2031 in the coming days, these are Bellingham’s best days. At the start of the season Mourinho had said: “He’s a No 10. He can’t play … well, he can play as a 6 or an 8, but then you lose him being closer to goal and I like that Jude.” Yet while there has been a shift this can still feel like the Jude that is everywhere too, the kid who was once handed the No 22 shirt because he was a 10, an 8 and a 4 all together , a player who can’t be stopped as he strides towards the area, opponents flying off him when he turns, like a catherine wheel spinning through midfield.
“He’s very special,” Silva told TNT. “He is a player that can create something very different at any moment like today. Physically he is very strong, the way he keeps the ball, the way he allows us to attack, the way he drives with the ball. He is good at everything. He is a complete player.”
Mourinho described him as “an extraordinary player”. He said: “Jude has everything: the physique, the technical ability, the understanding of the play, vision … everything. He is the best midfielder in the world. He changed the game. He is a natural leader, he makes huge demands of himself: you see that every day in the way he trains. He doesn’t hide his frustration when things don’t go well but he combats that with work, by putting the machine to work.”
Unleashed and undroppable, he has seven goals and five assists, as if it is even about that, however absurd the latest one was. Few, if any, footballers are playing better anywhere. Even if asked about the Ballon d’Or – yes, already – Bellingham replied that he doesn’t care about that, claiming that’s a journalists’ thing.
“I have a bit more experience now: there’s the coach, the staff, the confidence I have from the World Cup,” he said, speaking to the media in English and Spanish. “My Spanish is getting better, although I get a bit nervous with you. It’s easier in the changing room where I can say bad words. I’m loving it here. For English players, it’s such a good thing to play abroad.”
texts.https://www.dw.com/en/why-indian-nationa:
Whether through deception or desperation, Indians continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine. What can New Delhi do to protect its citizens from ending up fighting in Ukraine?
Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India's northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory.
But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces .
After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war.
In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified.
He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024 .
At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued.
In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine .
Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing.
The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone.
The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention.
Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. "This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the ministry said.
Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection.
"Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation," Trigunayat told DW.
He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries.
"Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents," Trigunayat said.
The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status.
Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine.
He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India .
"Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It's a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment," Sufiyan told DW.
Sufiyan's experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war.
Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military.
"Some of them, they don't join the army, but they end up in the army region. They're caught in the crossfire," Kumar told DW.
He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. "Russia is very cooperative so far," he said.
India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists.
The recruitment efforts reflect Russia's need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine , and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries.
Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin 's need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner.
He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest.
"In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that," said Khan.
Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home.
"For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable," he said.

Murat Mısırlı, 1968 yılında İzmir'in Karşıyaka ilçesinde doğdu. İlkokul yıllarından itibaren sporla ilgilenen Mısırlı, gençliğinde tenis, judo ve hentbol dallarında amatör ve profesyonel olarak faaliyet gösterdi. İstanbul Üniversitesi'nde mühendislik eğitimi aldığı sırada gelen modellik tekliflerini değerlendiren Mısırlı, 1990'lı yıllarda Türkiye'nin tanınmış erkek mankenlerinden biri oldu.
Mısırlı, profesyonel dansçılık da yaptı. Yurt dışında düzenlenen organizasyonlarda Türkiye'yi 30 farklı ülkede temsil etti. Güzellik yarışmalarının ve defilelerin koreografi çalışmalarında görev aldı. Oyunculuk kariyerine de adım atan Murat Mısırlı, Levent Kırca Tiyatrosu'nda sahneye çıktı ve çeşitli televizyon dizilerinde rol aldı. Burcu Ergün Mısırlı ile evli olan eski mankenin Tibet adında bir oğlu bulunuyor.

İstemli kaslar çiğneme, yürüme ve konuşma gibi hareketlerin yapılmasında görevlidir. ALS hastalığı ilerleyicidir ve belirtiler zamanla kötüleşme eğilimi gösterir. Altın fiyatlarında satış baskısı sürüyor. Ons altın çarşamba sabahı 3 bin 546 dolara gerilerken, geçen cuma görülen 14 ayın en düşük seviyesi yeniden piyasaların gündemine oturdu. Peki altın neden düşüyor? Altının düşmesine neden olan 3 etken uzmanlar tarafından açıklandı.
Ons altın, 25 Kasım Çarşamba sabahı saat 07.40 itibarıyla bir önceki kapanışa göre yüzde 0,15 değer kaybederek 3 bin 546 dolardan alıcı buldu. Bu seviye, geçen cuma görülen 3 bin 502 dolarlık dip noktaya yalnızca 44 dolar uzaklıkta. Piyasada şimdi konuşulan soru, o dibin yeniden test edilip edilmeyeceği.
İç piyasada da tablo farklı değil. Gram altın aynı saatlerde 5 bin 776 TL seviyelerinde işlem görüyor. Yatırımcıların gözü ise haftanın en kritik verisi olarak görülen ABD PCE fiyat endeksinde. Fed'in enflasyonu izlerken baktığı bu gösterge, faiz patikasına dair beklentileri doğrudan değiştirebilecek güçte.
Altındaki geri çekilmenin başını Fed çekiyor. Son günlerde Fed yetkililerinden gelen şahin mesajlar, ek faiz artırımı beklentisini güçlendirdi. Piyasa fiyatlamalarına göre aralık toplantısında 25 baz puanlık artış ihtimali yüzde 96 civarında; ocak ayında yeni bir artış da masada.
Faiz getirisi sunmayan altın için bu tablo kötü haber anlamına geliyor. Faizler yükseldikçe mevduat ve tahvil gibi getirili araçlar cazip hale geliyor, sarı metali elde tutmanın maliyeti ise artıyor. Altının son haftalardaki zayıf seyrinde bu beklentinin payı büyük.
İkinci neden borsalardan geliyor. Yapay zeka yatırımlarına yönelik endişeler teknoloji hisselerinde satış dalgasını tetikledi ve piyasalarda likidite baskısı arttı. Nvidia CEO'su Jensen Huang'ın etkisiyle başlayan toparlanma kısa sürede sönünce altın da yeniden aşağı yönlü hareket etti. Borsada kaybeden yatırımcıların nakde dönmek için altın pozisyonlarını bozması, düşüşü derinleştiren etkenlerden biri olarak görülüyor.
Üçüncü neden ise Washington'da. Trump yönetimi, ABD Yüksek Mahkemesi'nin iptal ettiği gümrük vergilerinin yerine yeni bir tarife planı hazırlıyor. Yeni vergi tehditleri Asya borsalarında, özellikle çip ağırlıklı piyasalarda sert düşüşlere yol açtı.
Diğer değerli metaller de kayıpta. Gümüşün onsu sabah saatlerinde yüzde 0, 29 düşüşle 40,70 dolardan işlem gördü. Platin yüzde 1,39 gerileyerek bin 258 dolara, paladyum ise yüzde 0,14 düşüşle 852 dolara indi.

Gök, Uluğ'un birçok projesinde müzisyen ve aranjör olarak yer aldı, yani ikili yalnızca aşkta değil sahnede de aynı yolda yürüyor.
Derya Uluğ, sevgilisi Asil Gök'ün 35'inci yaş gününde de romantik bir paylaşım yapmıştı. Şarkıcı bu paylaşımda Gök için 'Hayatımın dönüm noktası' ifadesini kullanmıştı.
Çiftin evlilik yolundaki ilk büyük adımı bu yılın şubat ayında geldi. Derya Uluğ, doğum gününde Asil Gök'ten sürpriz bir evlilik teklifi aldı ve mutluluğunu sosyal medya hesabından 'I Said Yes!' notuyla duyurdu.
Teklifin ardından ikinci adım da gecikmedi. Çift, haziran ayında aileleri ve yakın dostlarının katıldığı sade bir törenle nişanlandı. Gecenin en çok konuşulan detayı ise geleneksel tuzlu kahve seremonisi oldu. Derya Uluğ, daha önce vazgeçmeyeceğini söylediği bu adeti sürdürdü ve Asil Gök için bol tuzlu bir kahve hazırladı.
Derya Uluğ, ağustos ayında muhabirlerin sorularını yanıtlarken düğün planlarını da paylaşmıştı. Şarkıcı, 'Allah'tan bir mani olmazsa 2027 yılına evli olarak gireceğiz. Yılbaşından önce, önümüzdeki 4 ay içerisinde sade, sevdiklerimiz ve ailemizle birlikte olacağımız mutlu bir akşam hayal ediyoruz' demişti.
Bu planın ardından çiftin 25 Kasım'da nikah masasına oturması bekleniyor. Düğün hazırlıkları sürerken sade ve samimi bir organizasyon planlandığı ifade ediliyor.
Nikah öncesinde kına gecesi yapan Derya Uluğ, geceye kırmızı, uzun bir elbiseyle katıldı. Saçındaki kırmızı aksesuarla geleneksel konsepte uyum sağlayan şarkıcı, elinde tüyler ve çiçeklerle süslenmiş, üzerinde 'Derya'nın Kınası' yazan tefle poz verdi. Paylaşılan karede mutluluğu yüzüne yansıdı.
Geceden paylaşım yapan isimler arasında şarkıcı Ece Seçkin de vardı. Hamile olan Seçkin, kına gecesinden bir kareyi sosyal medya hesabından paylaştı.

Ons altın , yüzde 1,63 düşüşle 3 bin 499,02 dolara gerileyerek Eylül 2025'ten bu yana ilk kez 3 bin 500 doların altına indi. ABD Merkez Bankası'nın ( Fed ) faiz artırımı beklentilerinin güçlenmesi, doların değer kazanması ve küresel piyasalardaki satış dalgası altın fiyatları üzerinde baskı oluşturdu.
Altın fiyatlarındaki düşüşte en önemli etkenlerden biri Fed'in para politikasına ilişkin beklentiler oldu. Fed yetkililerinden gelen şahin mesajlar, ABD Merkez Bankası'nın aralık ayında faiz artırabileceği beklentisini güçlendirdi.
CME FedWatch verilerine göre piyasalarda Fed'in aralık toplantısında 25 baz puanlık faiz artırımı yapma ihtimali yüzde 96,4 seviyesinde fiyatlanıyor. Faiz getirisi bulunmayan altın, yüksek faiz ortamında yatırımcılar açısından daha az cazip hale geliyor.
ABD dolarının değer kazanması da ons altındaki düşüşü destekleyen unsurlar arasında yer alıyor. Doların güçlenmesi, dolar üzerinden fiyatlanan altını diğer para birimlerini kullanan yatırımcılar için daha pahalı hale getirerek talebi sınırlıyor.
Altın fiyatlarını baskılayan bir diğer gelişme küresel hisse senedi piyasalarında yaşanan satışlar oldu. Özellikle yapay zeka ve teknoloji hisselerinde görülen kayıplar, yatırımcıların nakit ihtiyacını artırdı.
Reuters'ın haberine göre, hisse senedi piyasalarındaki düşüş nedeniyle bazı yatırımcılar zararlarını karşılamak ve teminat ihtiyaçlarını gidermek amacıyla altın ve gümüş pozisyonlarını da kapattı. Bu durum, güvenli liman olarak görülen altının da satış baskısıyla karşılaşmasına yol açtı.
Dünya Altın Konseyi verilerine göre küresel altın destekli ETF varlıkları, 20 Kasım haftasında 4 bin 247 tona gerileyerek ekim sonunda görülen 4 bin 275 tonluk rekor seviyenin altına indi. Bu gelişme de yatırımcı talebindeki zayıflamaya işaret etti.
